subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO CHANGES TO PATENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by many people in southern Manitoba who are presently represented by Conservative Members of Parliament in the House of Commons, but only until the next election.
The petitioners are concerned about the Government's intention to change the Patent Act with regard to the purchase of prescription drugs. They believe this will result in higher costs to provincial Governments through their drug plans. They also believe it is unfair to Canadians whose health needs require the purchase of prescription drugs on an ongoing basis and this is being done at the expense of average Canadians because of the Government's wish to accommodate the United States in the free trade negotiations.
Therefore, the petitioners humble pray and call upon Parliament to reject these proposals which will increase prescription drug prices for Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to begin the debate on the two-hour time allocation motion with respect to Bill C-18. While I have only recently come to the transport dossier I do not think that in my entire eight years here on the Hill have I seen a Bill that has had more consultation and had more evidence given about it by witnesses than Bill C-18. In my entire eight years I have never seen a Bill that has been so well briefed. I would like to pay a compliment to the members of the Standing Committee on all sides of the House who worked very hard on this Bill.
I wish to emphasize that the Government places a high priority on transportation. Bills C-18, C-19 and C-21 reinforce that high priority. The over-all objective of Bill C-18 is summarized in Clause 3 of the Bill. It is to create the conditions necessary for a safe, adequate, effective and efficient transportation system that best serves the needs of shippers and travellers. The promotion of greater competition among carriers will improve efficiency and effectiveness in the transportation sector. This will make Canadian products more competitive in both domestic and international markets.
I am sure that most Canadians do not appreciate that, on average, our cost of transportation is 1 per cent to 2 per cent higher than costs in other countries and that, on average, the cost of transportation across the country is about 6 per cent. However, in some industries such as potash and other resource industries the cost can rise to as high as between 20 per cent and 30 per cent. I know that in the case of certain types of coal the cost of transportation can be as high as 50 per cent. Thus while we live in a huge country and cannot get away from such costs the fact of the matter is that we can reduce them so that the over-all effectiveness of our system is maximized.
Since I only have 10 minutes 1 want Hon. Members to appreciate the extent of consultation that has gone into Bill C-18. The reforms were forged as a result of extensive consultation with shippers, carriers, labour, the travelling public and other levels of government. This process commenced in early 1985. The previous Minister of Transport, now the esteemed Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), set in motion a two-pronged process, that is, a policy review and consultation with those interested in transportation.
The result of that long consultation was a position paper entitled Freedom to Move which was released in July, 1985. That paper proposed a comprehensive set of reforms of economic regulation of each mode of transportation. The document was widely distributed. It provoked many critical but thoughtful responses. The Minister and his officials continued to meet with as many people as possible to clarify
viewpoints and suggestions. In addition, the Freedom to Move paper was referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.
The Standing Committee heard the views of many witnesses, both in Ottawa and across the country. It produced a report recommending modifications and improvements to the White Paper Freedom to Move. Because of the concerns about the regulation of air services for our northern and remote communities the committee subsequently visited the North and produced a further report on that part of transportation. Based on all of this feedback in over 500 individual meetings, innumerable briefs and the committee's report, the Bill was drafted as Bill C-18 and was tabled in the House last June.
The extensive round of consultations was repeated and, after second reading approval in principle, the Bill was sent to the Standing Committee which again entered into a broad process, including hearing from witnesses across the country. Over 400 witnesses who made their views known with respect to this legislation appeared before the Standing Committee. Then, during clause-by-clause study the committee introduced several significant improvements.
As a result, I am personally convinced that this Bill represents a balanced package of reforms. The needs and interests of both the users and providers of transportation services will be well served by this Bill because they have had an opportunity to contribute at each and every stage of its development.
No Bill is ever perfect for all times since the economy and the Canadian way of life are constantly changing. I think one of the greatest additions to the Bill is that there will be annual reports on how the Bill is progressing and how the economy is adapting to it. There will be a comprehensive review at the end of four years. Personally, I think that is all we can do as legislators.
The Bill had enormous consultation before a White Paper was produced. The White Paper was then widely distributed and consulted upon, after which the Bill was introduced. The Standing Committee crossed the country again, heard all the views that were to be heard and then made some significant changes. Surely that is sufficient for the Bill. 1 think that this time allocation motion will pass. I hope Members will agree with me that the Bill has had sufficient consultation so that we can get on to finish report stage and third reading and get it out as the law of the land. As a result of the annual reports during the first four-year comprehensive review we can make whatever changes are necessary.
As I reflect on these regulatory reforms in transportation I see five or six guiding principles. Safety is the first priority. The committee in all its deliberations directed that safety regulations be improved. Second, transportation exists to serve the needs of shippers and travellers. In the past the nation has succumbed to the temptation that transportation is an end in itself as opposed to merely a service to shippers and travellers, to more efficiently ship goods across the country so that we
June 15, 1987

can put our products at tide water at a price level that is competitive with other countries.
We must never forget that over 30 per cent of our GNP comes from trade with other nations. Every time we spend $10, $3 of it has come from other countries. If we do not remain competitive with those other countries we will lose that $3 and our standard of living could drop by 30 per cent to 50 per cent practically overnight if we do not keep our transportation system running efficiently.
The third principle is that we need greater reliance on market forces and less reliance on economic regulation, a situation that will lead to more innovation and more enterprise, and a more competitive transportation system, both intramodally and intermodally. As a result of past regulation, competition within the various modes and certainly between the various modes has been distorted. This Bill would go a long way toward lessening that regulation-caused distortion.
Another principle is that, whenever necessary, the public interest must be protected through continued economic regulation. That is truer in the North than anywhere else, where there is a much smaller population, and more fragile markets. The Government has accepted the principle that we need to continue regulation in the North.
Wherever there is going to be regulation, another principle of the Bill is that it should be open, accessible, and not costly. All of us have had the occasion to talk to companies which have almost gone bankrupt as a result of bringing applications before the CTC in an effort to bring about more efficient and wider-ranging operations. That is just not the way regulation should operate. Under this Bill, the cost of regulation will be very much reduced.
Widespread consultation with all interested parties has produced a balanced package of reforms, a package which will best serve the needs of shippers and travellers while at the same time providing a good economic climate for efficient well-managed carriers.
Under this Bill, there are no losers. This Bill is clearly a win-win situation.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again, the Government has taken the easy way out. Once again, it has preferred to cut short debate instead of facing the widespread criticism of this Bill. Once again, it has decided to gag the Opposition. The Government has made a nasty habit of this. It imposed closure to pass a Bill that would benefit the oil multinationals. It imposed closure to pass a Bill that would benefit the multinational drug companies. And now, it is imposing closure for a Bill that is definitely biased towards this country's major shippers.
Mr. Speaker, I maintain that because we are talking about deregulation of our transportation industry, the Government's
National Transportation Act, 1986
decision is entirely unacceptable. I agree that the transportation industry is of vital importance to the development of the Canadian economy. That is why we say the Government should have consulted more and listened to those who testified against this Bill before the various parliamentary committees, instead of listening only to associations controlled by the big rich shippers, as the Government did. It should listen to the small shippers from the Maritimes and Western Canada who told us, for instance, that confidential contracts on domestic traffic might make them go out of business.
The Government should have listened to the unions that pointed out how many jobs would be lost in the industry if the Government persisted in its single-minded pursuit of deregulation.
The Government should have listened to professionals in the aviation industry, included pilots and others, who testified before the Transport Committee and told us in no uncertain terms that deregulation would unavoidably lead to a reduction in the quality of service and, even more important, in safety.
Representatives of the railway sector-both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific-told the Government that Bill C-18 was a threat to their survival.

The railroads told us that by opening up the Canadian market to competition from the American railways we would be reducing revenues, and investment in equipment and plant would suffer, leading in turn to a reduction in service and safety.
Did this Government listen? No, not at all.

Instead, he decided to set totally unrealistic deadlines, both for the Committee when it was considering the White Paper "Freedom to Move" and during consideration of Bill C-18 itself. Even now, at the report and third reading stage, we are still being saddled with absolutely unacceptable deadlines. The Government has systematically opted for closure just to please a few big Canadian shippers.
This Government has no regard for the democratic consultation process. Even worse, the transportation industry and thousands of Canadian workers will pay dearly for the Conservative Government's total lack of concern.
Mr. Speaker, when revising a general act that is so fundamental to the socio-economic well being of this country, the Government should have taken a more thoughtful approach.
During the debate on second reading, we in the Official Opposition, we in the Liberal Party said that considering the changes being sought, the Government could at least have taken steps to measure the impact of deregulation on such areas as: traveller safety; consumers, especially in connection with air transportation rates; employment in the industry; acceptable levels of foreign control; and finally, impact on regional development.

June 15, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
In all five areas, the Government has not budged an inch. We hoped it would use clause-by-clause consideration in committee to make some changes. We on our side suggested a number of amendments to improve the Bill. Unfortunately, the Conservative majority on the Committee, obeying the signals from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, systematically refused any changes that made sense in social and economic terms.
On the subject of regional development, for instance, the Government rejected an amendment by the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud) which would have given some political clout to the statement of principles contained in Clause 3 (d) of the Bill.
As for employment, a measure aimed at protecting workers, which I proposed, was rejected. Regarding confidential contracts, I think we should listen to what was said by Prairie Malt Limited, a small Saskatchewan shipper, when he appeared before the Committee, and I quote:

We are of the opinion that the suggested confidentiality in rate setting will work out to the serious detriment of small and medium companies competing within a given industrial sector with large and more powerful conglomerates. Confidential rate negotiations on contracts will almost surely enable physically well-situated and financially flexible industrial entities-especially those with more than one plant site-to utilize transportation contracts, and through them the railways themselves, to serve as marketing tools-or, to say it stronger, as accomplices in power-plays-against smaller competitors.
We tried to deal with that concern, Mr. Speaker, by ensuring that confidential contracting could only occur on transborder traffic. The Government refused.
The Government has been totally inflexible in crafting this legislation, legislation which is totally and unequivocally biased toward the large conglomerates in Canada.
It is a disgrace that this Government has not taken into account the over-all interests of Canadians, whether involving small, medium or large expenditures, taking into account an industry that has, throughout the years, been prosperous.
The transportation industry in Canada is a good industry. It is an industry that provides well-paying employment. Bill C-18 is a threat to the prosperity of the transportation industry. That is a point that has been made by the railways, by the trucking associations, and observers of the airline industry.
Why is the Government moving so rapidly and vigorously in this direction? It is incredible. There is no possibility for us in the Opposition to stop the Government. We are awaiting the result of this catastrophe a few years down the line. When we have another chance to form the Government, we will certainly amend legislation which already will have been very bad for the workers, the transportation industry, and the Canadian public at large.

Madam Speaker, the Government's decision-I bow to the Chair, I see that you have taken over from your colleague, Madam Speaker-the Government's decision to introduce time limitation is the logical result of a process that reflects the lack of courage and political maturity of a Government that is practically hand in glove with the "big guys" in our society.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the whole effort by the Government to deregulate transportation for the past 2.5 years has been nothing but a litany of intransigence. The past and present Ministers have said that the Bill was not engraved in stone, that they would be flexible, that they would listen, and that they were open to amendments, et cetera. As far as I can recall, I think they have accepted one amendment in the House and two amendments in committee.
It all started with Freedom to Move, the government White Paper on transportation. The Government did not want the committee to travel. It took a lot of pressure from scores of organizations and Members of the House to get the Government to agree to committee travel.
The committee went to four places in Canada-Vancouver, Winnipeg, Halifax, and Ottawa. It left out the villages of Montreal and Toronto! It left out all the northern territories and all northern parts of the provinces. It did not go near southwestern Ontario.
It makes one wonder why the Government is in such a hurry. It brought in a Bill in the previous session which remained on the Order Paper for some 13 months. Then, in the next session of Parliament it was given a new number and was placed on the Order Paper again. The Government called it for debate, and we had four partial days at second reading in principle, on closure. It then went to the standing committee, and we had to fight, argue, and plead continually-not only us but scores of organizations, companies, and individuals-for the committee to travel to a number of locations.
The committee went to nine locations-Vancouver, Edmonton, Regina, Winnipeg, St. John's, Halifax, Moncton, Montreal, and Ottawa. At least 36 places were worthy of consideration to hold parliamentary hearings and hear witnesses. I submitted a list of locations and thought if we could get to at least 16 or 20 of them that would suffice.
Again the Government refused to allow the committee to go to Yellowknife or Whitehorse. It wouldn't go to Labrador or to any of the northern parts of the provinces. The municipalities, the trade union movement, and the forest industry wanted hearings in Prince George and Prince Rupert in northern British Columbia and got none. The southern half of the Province of Alberta was left out, and I think the committee heard from one witness from the Peace River country. There should have been a hearing in Dawson Creek, British Columbia to cover the Peace River country. The committee should have gone to Dauphin or Thompson in northern
June 15, 1987

Manitoba. It should have at least gone to Thunder Bay and Sudbury in northern Ontario.
There have been at least five dozen requests from boards of trade, city and town councils, and trade union groups in southwestern Ontario asking for hearings. They did not get them.
The Government put a time limit on when the committee had to report. It reported within the time limit ordered by the House, and the report sat for six weeks before the Bill was called for report stage consideration. Suddenly the Government is in a big hurry.
The Parliamentary Secretary said that the legislation would increase competition, competitiveness, et cetera. When the Freedom to Move hearings started, there were six relatively large regional airlines and two national carriers. Now we have two, and the Government says that there will be more competition. Those two carriers will control something in the order of 80 per cent to 90 per cent of all airline traffic through their major national networks as well as the operating and licensing agreements for a bunch of little feeder airlines all over Canada. They control it, and the Government tells us that there will be more competition. Competition has been reduced by two-thirds.
The Government talks about confidential contracts and confidential freight rates. If there were anything more anticompetitive than secret deals between large corporate shippers and one or two railroads, I do not know what it would be. No one is about to build another railroad; there are only two of them in Canada.
The trucking industry asked for a delay of at least one year until all things were in place. The Parliamentary Secretary said that safety was a number one priority and that there would be no compromise on safety. We have heard that from both Ministers; we have heard it ad nauseam.
Where is the railway safety board? Where is the rail safety Act? Where is the board on highway trucking safety? Where is the legislation, the regulations, and rules for that? All those things will take at least a year to implement.
The aviation safety board has just been established for a year. It is still setting up, and we do not have all the regulations governing it.
The Canadian Trucking Association pleaded with us not to proceed until all these things were in place-safety, security, proper regulations, and the people necessary to enforce them, such as inspectors and what not.
We have three amendments on the Order Paper, and the Government does not want us to get to them. There is one it will not be able to avoid. I call them the Fred Turner amendments. They would guarantee that never again could the new transportation agency, the air safety board-whoever will administer the Aeronautics Act, or whoever inherits the duties of the air transport committee of the CTC-do what was done to Fred Turner, bankrupt his airline because he was late filing
National Transportation Act, 1986
his statistical reports. The Government admitted that there had been 1,600 occasions when airlines or aircraft operators were late filing their reports.
We are anxious to have these matters dealt with in the House, but the Government does not want to deal with them; it is afraid. It refuses to listen to witnesses. It said that it would be open and that it would consult. It heard witnesses but it did not listen.
We want the legislation to establish appeal procedures so that operators have some protection and some rights, so that they cannot be victims of bureaucratic overkill or the Government ignoring them. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) became involved in this one. Mr. Turner has been haunting the House of Commons for almost four months. Members of Parliament from all three Parties support him, but the Government refuses to act. It offered a $15,000 payment without prejudice. It bankrupted the man. He lost five aircraft, his hangar, and all his equipment. He is scheduled to lose his house next month. The Government offers $15,000, which in itself is an admission of guilt. It is a pittance. All Mr. Turner is asking for is an independent arbitrator to hear his case and the government side of the story and make a decision. Mr. Turner has filed a lawsuit in the courts. The Government is now saying, "Well, you can't sue us". First the Government said "Go ahead and sue". Mr. Turner cannot afford a lawyer for one day, let alone the months and months a lawsuit would take. I am confident that with a reasonable settlement put forward by an independent arbitrator there will be no court case. The Government can afford to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars and can spend months and years in court at the expense of an innocent individual Canadian citizen.
It is patent nonsense that all of a sudden the Government is in a big hurry. Three full days on report stage would have finished all the amendments and half a day would have been sufficient on third reading. That would not be unreasonable. We were proceeding with all dispatch dealing with amendments during the one day we have had so far. We have had a dozen or 14 motions dealt with and out of the way. It would take two more days to deal with each one of them. Why will the Government not let us have that time, Madam Speaker? Why did the Government take so long to get to work on the Bill? Why is the Government all of a sudden in a big hurry? It is bludgeoning Parliament into accepting bad legislation while we have amendments trying to make a bad Bill less bad.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a privilege to speak today on the subject of Bill C-18. I feel that the issue of this Bill will have a favourable impact for the shippers and for the citizens of my province of Alberta and western Canada generally.
I listened with interests to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and I found it hard to believe that he indeed was a westerner speaking the way he did. This Bill is to the ultimate benefit of ordinary citizens, to small and

June 15, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
medium businesses and to the people of western Canada generally. It is about competition and fairness and the restoration of justice. It goes a long way to cap the well known well-springs of discontent in western Canada and it leads toward that noblest of all goals, national reconciliation. I believe that the socialist alliance with the CPR will result in some electoral bringing into account come 1989.
I have received voluminous correspondence from the citizens of Alberta on the subject of this Bill. A typical example is one received recently from an employee of Alberta Gas Chemicals in Medicine Hat, which letter in part reads:
-we currently ship approximately 90 per cent of our product by rail. As I am sure you are aware competition is the essence of good business. Without competition there is no need to be efficient and you can demand whatever the traffic will bear for your product or service.
With Competitive Line Rates we will be able to be more competitive on pricing of our Methanol which should allow us to sell and ship more product.
If Bill C-18 does not pass, we are in a position where without fair competitive freight rates we could go out of business. If we are forced out of business, it will mean a loss of approximately 100 jobs at AGCL in Medicine Hat for a starter. If we go out of business, that means the CPR, locally, will probably also have lay-offs as there will be approximately 400 to 800 fewer rail cars to ship each month from Medicine Hat.
It is employment we are talking about, Madam Speaker. It is also justice in terms of freight rates.
I have a letter from a constituent in Edmonton:
I have been involved on more than one occasion with respect to encouraging incoming businesses. After the second look at expenses at the freighting end of production the early enthusiasm pales and we are again losers.
1 believe that it is imperative that we have a drastic change in the freight rates for western Canada.
I have a note from the Alberta Government:
Rail provides the life-force for many landlocked Alberta manufacturers and producers. Their products and distance from markets make them dependent on rail.
In 1985, Alberta generated 48 million tonnes of freight for CN and CP, 20 per cent of their total business. Sixty per cent of this came from producers that are captive to rail and in most cases captive to one carrier.
Under existing legislation, rail carriers are comparatively free from market competition. The rates they choose can create winners and losers in Alberta's major commodity industries.
The results of this are clear. In 1982, Alberta related shipments generated 28 per cent of the total system of traffic that paid over 70 per cent of the total contribution to railway constant costs for Canada.
The rates applied to Alberta rail shippers for the past several years have been increasing faster than railway costs. Rates offered to captive shippers have received a disproportionate share of this increase.
I will continue with a note from the Hinton, Alberta District Chamber of Commerce:
We are very concerned, at this time, because it is our understanding that CN, a Crown corporation, and the CP whose relationship within this country parallels the CNs are both amassing a fierce lobby against the competitive line rates provisions of this Bill.
We are a resource-based community depending on pulp, paper and coal; a western Canadian community whose welfare and survival is dependent upon exporting our goods to national and international markets. Because our community is located in western Canada, we are disadvantaged in our ability to compete due to this fact. The transportation component in exporting our goods to those market does not and will not reflect market conditions as long as the CN and CP have for all intents and purposes a monopoly. Subsidies are
not our forte, however, we cannot and will not stand by and see our only hope to enhance our ability to compete in the market-place dashed by a Crown corporation and, if I may say, "A semi-Crown Corporation".
The whole concept of this Bill is to assure employees and shippers that safety will be maintained and that the benefits of deregulation will redound and that the disadvantages will not prevail. Safety we know is a major priority for all those involved in transportation. This legislation is a product of the viewpoints and ideas advanced over a very extensive cross Canada consultative process over the past two years involving contact with over 450 groups and organizations.
I would venture to say that the reverse is the case of that painted by the Hon. Member for Regina West. Consultation has been of the essence in the drafting and in the amendment of this Bill. Those consultations involved labour, users, business, transportation companies, the travelling public and provincial and territorial governments. In addition, of course, there were the hearings of the standing committee to which the Hon. Member referred.
I would like to touch on a submission from Sultran Ltd. based in Calgary. This is not a minor player.
-Sultran ships up to six million tonnes of sulphur per year from 14 Alberta plants and three northeastern British Columbia plants to Vancouver for export. This volume generates about $200 million a year in rail freight.
Because of its relatively low value and long distances to tidewater, sulphur is effectively captive to rail transport, and generally captive to one carrier.
Since there is neither an effective transport alternative nor effective economic regulation control over railway rates, the railways are, at present, free to engage in monopoly pricing. Bill C-18 remedies this condition by introducing competitive provisions which attempt to limit the monopoly power of railways over captive commodities and at locations served by only one carrier.
This new policy statement in the Bill provides that all carriers must meet acceptable safety standards, that competition and market forces are to be the prime agent in determining price and service levels, that government intervention will occur only when necessary to protect the public interest, but carriers are to be fairly compensated for any imposed public duty, and carriers pricing policies are not to be discriminatory.
Canadians have imbued within them an innate sense of fairness and Canadians react in a rather forceful manner when they feel that they are being discriminated against. This piece of legislation responds to that sense of discrimination which has bedevilled western Canadians, and I submit, other Canadians for the past century. It gives, for the first time, to western Canadians the opportunity to compete on a level playing field with their brothers and sisters in central and eastern Canada. Thus, I am saddened when I hear Members opposite decrying this legislation. The Minister has responded to Members opposite and has agreed to a number of amendments. These amendments have accommodated the major objections that were raised when the Bill was first introduced.
This piece of legislation will bring to Alberta and to western
Canada a response to the needs of users of transportation
services. Our ability to expand markets will depend upon our
June 15, 1987

ability to produce goods and services at the lowest possible costs.
Of particular importance to my province are the provisions of the legislation relating to railway freight transportation. The long distances to markets for exports and the dominance of one major carrier in the northern part of the province and another in the south has limited alternatives available to shippers for transporting products. The current National Transportation Act provides rail carriers with considerable pricing freedoms and little incentive to compete while provisions to protect shippers against excessive rail rates have proven ineffective. As a result, the province incurs a significant freight rate burden.
If Alberta is to maintain its position in increasingly competitive world markets, this burden must be reduced. The provisions of this Bill to increase competition between carriers and to provide shippers with more effective mechanisms for resolving rate disputes with carriers go a long way toward allowing this to be accomplished.
In view of the criticism the Bill has received from railways, labour unions and the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), there are a few points that I would like to address in concluding. First, there is no direct causal relationship between deregulation and safety in the Canadian context. Regulations pertaining to safety are not changed adversely in this Bill. In fact, they are augmented. Recent changes to strengthen aeronautic safety and the proposed new rail safety Bill should address safety concerns.
Second, there is the principle of the railway's desire to reduce costs. However, with the exception of branch lines which are covered in the new legislation, the railways have not been specific on what legislation or regulation they believe should be changed.
The legislative package contained in Bill C-18 addresses concerns of westerners expressed since the time of the 1973 Western Economic Opportunities Conference. We in the West believe that the quick passage of this legislation is vital. A key provision in the legislation for many shippers in Alberta and indeed in the rest of Canada is the mechanism for competitive line rates. This provision will allow shippers who are now captive to a single carrier to gain access to a competing alternate carrier for the movement of goods. Removal of this provision from the Bill would have eliminated a large part of the industry's support of the legislation and removal of such a proposal from the Bill as suggested by Members opposite would have gutted this piece of legislation.
In conclusion, I submit that this Bill should pass swiftly through all stages. The people of the West are waiting to see how the the House disposes of the Bill and are watching with great care to see how Members on all sides vote on this vital piece of legislation which will go a long way toward realizing the destiny of western Canada.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to offer some comments at
National Transportation Act, 1986
this point in the debate on Bill C-18. I have something more than a passing interest in the initiatives that are proposed because I do believe that the strengthening and augmenting of the transportation system of Canada is one of the primary responsibilities of any national Government.
Because of our geography and the peculiar nature of our economic system, it is very important that a national Government maintain a clear and overriding responsibility for the way we move people, goods and services across Canada. This should be done in a way that not only maximizes efficiency but also ensures that there is a maximum of service. That is why I find it so dismaying that the Government would impose a closure motion on this very important topic. This is a matter that requires a continuing and ongoing examination by Parliament in order to ensure that the legislation is right. It should not be approached in a way that would simply ensure that it meets the parliamentary timetable, but in a way that would ensure that the vast array of important interests across Canada are properly and effectively reflected in the legislation.
We do not change the Transportation Act that often, so when we do it we had better make sure that what we are doing is carefully conceived and integrated into a package that will respond, not only to contemporary needs but to future needs. That is why we object so strenuously to the fact that the very important evidence that was brought forward during the hearings of the Transport Committee was ignored in the Bill. We were not given the time or effort required to reconsider, reexamine and redefine the legislation.
Let me tell the House of one example of this that comes to mind. Three or four weeks ago I had the opportunity to meet with the national executive of the organization representing the physically handicapped in Canada. When I was Minister of Transport I felt that one of the most important contributions the national Government could make to alleviate the disadvantage suffered by those with various handicaps would be to ensure that the transportation system reflected their needs and concerns and was adapted in a way that would give them the kind of mobility they require to pursue their occupations and their rights as Canadians. We set forward a series of guidelines that we felt should be incorporated in the transportation system, and those guidelines should now be reflected in the legislation. However, they are not. It was clear from my discussions with the group representing the various organizations that speak for the handicapped that this would be an opportunity lost.
Members of Parliament should reflect on why they would support a closure motion to forestall any further examination of the legislation when it is clear that a major constituency is being ignored and in fact rejected as evidenced by the lack of measures put forward in the Bill. We must ask ourselves why the representations made by these organizations across Canada were treated with such indifference. We must ask why there was not a willingness during the consideration of this legislation in the House to take account of those representations and, even at this late date, to provide for a modification. It seems

June 15, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
that we are in an unfortunate position. The imperatives of political timetabling are taking precedence over the necessity for passing good legislation. It seems to me that what is before us is an indication of what has become all too common and frequent. It seems to be important to acquire a so-called list of accomplishments without really examining the substance, the details and the ramifications of those accomplishments. It seems to be far more important to get the headlines than to get the substance right. As my seatmate, the transportation spokesman for my Party, has said, the decision of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to impose a suffocation of the consideration of this Bill by the House stands as evidence of a clear and unmistakable calumny on the part of the Government, as evidence of its unwillingness to take its responsibilities seriously, considering the importance placed on this matter during the last election.
I will point to another reason why we should be examining this legislation with more thorough care than we will be able to because of the closure motion. Through a wide variety of activities we are observing the serious reduction of the powers and abilities of the national Government to form successfully an economic union to meet the imperatives of international competition. As I said earlier in my remarks, transportation is not only a clear responsibility of the national Government but should be even more seriously recognized when we are talking about giving the provinces further powers, when there is serious consideration of severe limitations of federal powers as a consequence of free trade negotiations, and when there is a move toward the privatization of various Crown corporations.
The collective impact of these initiatives is an erosion of the capacity of the national Government to meet effectively and successfully the national goals and objectives. That will not become apparent overnight, but in the months and years ahead as the country tries to respond to new demands this incredible move by the Conservative Government to disband the national Government's role in the economic and social life of the country will be decried. The Government may have to pay a price for that in the judgment of historians, but it should certainly be more carefully examined now.
I raise this concern, particularly in the field of transportation, because I can recall the discussions and negotiations of which I was a part when we were beginning to consider our own form of reforms in this field. One of the most important questions that we raised at that time was with regard to safety and whether deregulation afforded sufficient protection to maintain high quality standards and maintenance of the transportation system. We did not want to have the continuing problems with which we were faced in the rail, air and trucking industries with regard to the continuing incidents of danger and disaster. Yet there is nothing in this legislation or in the corollary of complementary moves of the Government to give assurance that there was a fair recognition of those facts.
Similarly, when we were considering the role of transportation we had to consider the role of regional development. That role cannot be judged only by the criteria, the accounts or the economists. We knew from the history of the country that if we were to maintain a national fabric we had to ensure that all parts of the country were involved. I must say that those have not been involved.
In the short time I have remaining I must say that this is an unfinished piece of legislation which requires much more examination and work. We can only regret the fact that the Government seems to be unwilling to give the people of Canada that opportunity.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I always considered the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) to be the father of this legislation. I thought that in his speech he would apologize to the House and the country for his sponsorship of the attempts by the previous Liberal Government to introduce a regime of deregulation in Canada.
I have a number of concerns with what is happening in the House at this time. Despite what you have heard from a number of the previous speakers, we are not actually debating Bill C-18 at this time. We are involved in the process of time allocation which limits debate on report stage and third reading of this very important piece of legislation. As you know, Madam Speaker, time allocation is just another way of saying closure. It is a way of cutting off debate, limiting the number of people who can participate in the debate, and guaranteeing that only a few of the proposed amendments are debated and voted upon by the House.
This is a very difficult process for the House. The Government cannot claim that we have instigated a filibuster on this piece of legislation. When this Bill was finally brought back to the House for debate we in the Opposition announced that we would move quickly to introduce all of our amendments in order that we could have a recorded vote on them in the House. We believe this is necessary because we have been told by government spokespersons that the Government is willing to accept some of the amendments standing in the name of the Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and in the name of one of the Liberal Members. However, the Government has refused to tell us which of those amendments it is willing to accept.
W'e are in an ironic situation. The Government, which says that it will accept some of the amendments but will not tell us which, is now introducing time allocation which will not allow us to reach some of the amendments which the Government may or may not favour. Talk about parliamentary democracy. I hear a voice from the wilderness, that of the Parliamentary Secretary, saying that we are stalling. We are not stalling. We have said that we would move as quickly as possible through the amendments. We said that we would forego debate on some of the amendments.
The first speaker from our Party on this time allocation
motion, the Member for Regina West, pointed out that with
June 15, 1987

two or three days at report stage we could deal with every one of the amendments. Two or three days debate is not very much to change fundamentally the way in which the transportation industry is regulated. That is the purpose of Parliament. We should ensure that our amendments, some of which are acceptable to the Government, are debated and voted upon. The Government's insinuation that we have been stalling is patently not true.
As the Member for Regina West said, the reason that this legislation is before the Elouse in the latter half of June is because the Government stalled. The Government took a year before finally introducing this legislation in the House. It took a second session of the House before the Government finally brought the legislation into the House for debate. After committee stage the Government delayed for weeks and weeks before introducing it for third reading. All of that speaks of the Government delaying this legislation, although it knows the legislation will be passed. What the Government is doing now is preventing a full debate and decision by this House.
One of the things we discovered was a government memorandum talking about lowering the public profile on free trade. The Cabinet had papers which suggested the Government should do all it could to make sure there was no public debate, that the public was not aroused or made aware of the implications of free trade. The Government was afraid that if that happened there would be even more opposition to the attempt to negotiate a free trade pact with the Americans. Obviously some industries and towns are going to be hurt and some people are going to lose their jobs under free trade. That was the Government strategy. It is following that same strategy with deregulation.
The Opposition has said it is not going to stall the legislation but we want to introduce the amendments and have them debated for a short time and then make a decision. Yet the Government, for its own reasons, has moved time allocation. It is completely unnecessary. This is a major piece of legislation. The Opposition has indicated a willingness to co-operate-not to bend over and play dead but to co-operate. That is the most the Government can expect when we are opposed to a piece of legislation. We are willing to co-operate but we are not willing to rush the legislation through the House.
We recognize that this legislation will fundamentally change the way the transportation industry works. It is ironic that in the long time it has taken the Government to move forward with this legislation-not the Opposition but the Government-we have seen less and less competition in Canada. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Regina West talked about the air transportation industry. We have had merger after merger lately, the most famous and most recent being CP and PWA getting married to form CAI or Canadian Airlines International. We know during that same period of time more and more management agreements came into place. CAI has agreements with Calm Air in northern Manitoba and Time
National Transportation Act, 1986
Air in parts of Alberta and B.C. Air Canada has management arrangements with a number of other feeder airlines. This has been done in such a way that competition is being further and further reduced.
Conservative Members speak about how we are going into a market economy and deregulation will expand the number of operators. We will have more service. Yet the facts show the exact opposite. By the time this legislation is passed we will be down to one or two airline conglomerates for the most part.
We have seen examples of how service can be altered. Just after the announcement that CP and PWA were merging, we had CP cutting its service to Yukon. Obviously; why should they compete against each other? The management and feeder systems in that airline are such that if you are coming from one of the more remote parts of Canada it is almost impossible to make connections with other airlines. You have to stay within that management system. That is good for their business and you expect them to do it, but it is going to get worse and worse.
It is not a matter of all of a sudden freeing up the system. There are problems with the CTC and over-regulation in some areas. There is no question about that. Yet we are taking away the protection of Government regulation and giving control to a small group of owner-operators, especially in the airline industry. We move from one monopoly-Government regulation, which at least allowed a number of different operators to be involved in a competitive sense-to a monopoly of the large airlines which will control the air transportation industry.
At the same time we know the Government intends to do what it can to privatize Air Canada. We have no idea what form that will take. Will the Government allow CAI to buy Air Canada? Will a system be in place such that Air Canada will not really be competing? Will those parts of Canada now served by Air Canada, on what may or may not be profitable runs, be in a situation where those runs will be cut once Air Canada is privatized?
Those are all legitimate questions which should be addressed and answered in this House before the legislation is allowed to pass. That is one of the reasons we are seeing a rush after so many months and months of delay. The Government wants the legislation passed before it has the courage to announce what it is doing with Air Canada.
I recognize I am out of time; that is one of the problems with this process. There is a lot in the transportation industry that concerns me and my constituents. I am afraid that the process the Government is using for its own political agenda is actually destroying the input of Parliament on a very important piece of legislation.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is a time for talk and there is a time for action. In my view we have talked enough about the Bill and it is now time to see what the Bill will do.

June 15, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
Every illustration the Opposition gave happened in a regulated society, not under Freedom To Move. Yet they want more regulation, particularly the NDP. Of course that is understandable. Socialists love regulations. They love to tell people what is good for them. That is part of their philosophy. The philosophy of this Party is to let the people speak and then carry out their wishes to the greatest possible degree. That is what we are trying to do.
The Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) said it took us too long. "There have been a lot of delays!" The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) said we are going too fast. Which is it, too slow or too fast? I do not think it is either. I think we are going at just about the right speed.
The Hon. Member talked about delays. What do they expect? We had week after week of committee meetings. We listened to everyone who came along. Then we sat day after day going over the scores of amendments brought forward by the Opposition, as well as some from the Government. That takes time. Should we not have done that? Is that what they are complaining about? Every amendment they presented was discussed. Then they complain because they cannot bring them back to the House. How much time do they want to waste? We set up a committee to go into the details, not so we could bring them all back here again. If we are going to do that, why have committees at all?
This Bill is an example of what should happen under a free enterprise Government. It removes not all but many of the shackles which have stopped free enterprise from working. That is why the NDP particularly is opposed to it. They love regulation. They want to tell the people what to do, when to do it, how to do it, and where to do it. This Government does not do that. We believe the people are mature and can make up their own minds. We will give them the opportunity to go into business without Government regulations and red tape. That is what this Bill does.
The Hon. Member from Regina, who is a member of the Committee, said we did not travel enough. Let me tell the House that in 1985 we travelled to Vancouver, Winnipeg and Halifax. I do not know how many briefs we received at every one of those hearings. That was under Freedom to Move. The Opposition says that we did not go to the North. In 1986 we went to Churchill, Rankin Inlet, Cambridge Bay, Yellowknife, Inuvik, and Whitehorse. This year we had hearings at Vancouver, Edmonton, Regina and Winnipeg, to say nothing of the days and days of hearings here in Ottawa. How much travelling does the Opposition want? Does it want to spend the whole year travelling at Government expense, or a whole month?
I think the Government has been pretty liberal in providing us with the amount of time it did, and I think the people of Canada appreciated it. We were thanked by the people who came to us from various places. They did not complain, because what we were doing was trying to give the people of
Canada a chance, to the greatest possible degree, to say what they thought about Freedom to Move. A majority of the people want Freedom to Move to come into being as fast as possible.
I wish I had with me today the letters and wires I received so that Hon. Members could see just how high the pile is, and they all say in effect, "Move it. Do not talk anymore. We want some action. The time for talking is over". I think Freedom to Move will be wonderful for the country. In the first place, it involves all modes of transportation from the pipelines to trains, from small airplanes to the mighty jets, from small trucks to 18 wheelers. It includes every type of transportation. One correspondent said this country is very far flung, in fact it is flung too far. But whatever way we look at it, Canada is a vast country and transportation is probably the number one essential which keeps our country together. We want transportation to be efficient.
We want transportation to not only do the job, we want it to cost the lowest cost possible to the consumer. The consumer is the one who pays in the final analysis. This Bill will help the shippers give better prices to the consumer. We are doing our utmost in this Bill to eliminate monopoly and replace it with competition. That is exactly what the Bill is designed to do.
This is the first time in the history of this nation that transportation for the regions has been included in a transportation Bill. We are not only concerned about the country as a whole, we are concerned about the people in various parts of the Maritimes, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. They have transportation problems and this Bill is designed not to ignore the problems but to look after them. There are regions in the west as well, in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba and in British Columbia, with regional transportation problems.
The Opposition said we did not listen to the North. A number of these submissions we received told us not to go too fast in the North because it has a sparse population and vast distances. They told us to go a little slower in the North, so the Government went a little slower. We established a line, and north of that line there will continue to be regulations, for the time being. We will work gradually into a Freedom to Move atmosphere. That is the principle upon which we are working.
We have set up a transport board which will look into all of these items and ensure that there is fairness and competition, and that we give every mode of transportation a chance to compete. Many times I have seen a regulated society stop people from investing their money in a service they thought they could provide better than anyone else. A transport board told them they could not do it. Under the regulated society the franchise would be give to one trucking firm and it could add truck after truck after truck and no one else could get in. It was not just a franchise, it was an monopoly. I have seen it happen scores of time. Individuals and small companies which wanted to go into the trucking business could not because the board would not let them. The Government bureaucrats said "No, you cannot do it. We have enough trucks in the system".
June 15, 1987

The new Bill will give the people a chance to act. If I want to invest my money in a small plane or truck or even a train, if I want to take a chance and compete with the big boys, all I have to do is meet the safety requirements. I must have proper insurance and meet safety standards, but if I have those, the Government will not say I cannot invest my money. The Government will say, "You make sure that you protect the public interests and that safety is looked after and then you can go to town and invest your money". I would have the right to lose and I would have the right to gain. Everyone who goes into business under a free enterprise system has that right. It is a right to win and a right to lose. They take the chance and if they lose it is on their own initiative, not on the initiative of some bureaucrat sitting in some office who perhaps never operated a business, never had to meet a payroll and never had to toe the mark in order to stay alive in the free enterprise system.
Let me say once again that this is good legislation for Canada. It removes some of the shackles which have stopped free enterprise from working. Watch it over the next few years it is going to do great things for our nation.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I regret that the Government has seen fit to introduce closure on report stage of this particular Bill, a move which removes from consideration a number of very serious, reasoned and careful amendments which had been put down by my Party in order to improve this Bill. The Bill is designed to revamp the National Transportation Act and its stated purpose is to increase competition in the transportation sector by removing certain regulations which hindered the ability to compete. It will affect rail, air and trucking.
The major economic benefit expected from the legislation is that Canadian goods and products will get to market more efficiently, faster, and in a less expensive way. This will include Canadian exports to the U.S. which the Government says will reach their destination at a lower cost, and therefore will be more competitive.
This is very laudable but, unhappily, the Government in its rush to get this Bill through has sacrificed consideration of amendments which would have improved the Bill. The Bill reflects, perhaps, a certain commitment to ideology over practicality. I want to mention some of the things about which we have concerns and on which we have amendments which the Government will not now consider.
To begin with, there is the introduction of confidential contracts. Under this Bill the railway companies, CN and CP, will be allowed to enter into confidential contracts with large bulk shippers. In other words, the rates charged by the railway company to the shipper remain confidential and do not have to be published. Any rebate or allowance provided by a railway company on a published rate must also remain confidential.
National Transportation Act, 1986
We in the Liberal Party were in favour of confidential contracts for transborder movements. We thought it would help to reduce the competitive advantage enjoyed by U.S. railways over CN and CP in transborder shipping rates and therefore enhance the competitiveness of our goods in U.S. markets.
We are not in favour of confidential contracts for domestic rates. It seems to us that what will happen is that the large bulk shippers will clearly benefit. They will be able to negotiate favourable low rates for their voluminous shipments. Railway company revenues will decrease and there will be a tendency to fill that gap at the expense of the small and medium-sized shippers who will end up cross-subsidizing the rate decreases to the large bulk shippers.
CP Rail, Canada's only other railway company apart from the federal Crown corporation CN, is of the view that in competing with CN to offer the lowest rate to shippers through confidential contracts it will not be able to absorb as much lost revenues as CN will be able to absorb and may in fact be forced out of business by the year 1992.
Our other concern is with respect to the trucking industry which is already suffering as a result of the Government's large increases in gasoline prices. Canadian trucking companies are already at a disadvantage in terms of competing with American trucking companies. They will certainly face unfair competition in this respect since they are not entitled to negotiate confidential contracts.
Another concern I have is with respect to foreign ownership since this Bill has no limitations on foreign takeovers of Canadian transportation companies. There are two guidelines in this respect. First, mergers and takeovers over $20 million and involving over 10 per cent of the voting shares of a Canadian transportation firm will be reviewed by the Governor in Council. Takeovers or mergers below those ceilings would be reviewed by Investment Canada. This means that very large takeovers will only be subject to political review, which leaves the potential for patronage decisions rather than decisions based on clear criteria which Canadians know, understand and accept. There is quite a risk that many good Canadian companies will pass into foreign hands.
Nowhere in the Bill is much concern shown for regional development. The concern is for competition, for market rates. In a country as vast as Canada clearly what will happen is that the centres that are profitable, such as those in the Montreal, Toronto, Windsor corridor, will be well serviced, while isolated communities in which there is not much traffic will increasingly find themselves with less and less service as time goes on, and as the only motive is profit. The history of our country shows that our transportation system has been used to aid regional development, and as a way of opening up communications links and trade links. This Bill will put an end to that.

June 15, 1987
National Transportation Act, 1986
Before us is a measure that has been protested by the Premiers and, in particular, the Council of Maritime Premiers. The Government has decided to ignore their recommendations.
We also have a great many concerns about safety. As an example, before us we have the U.S. deregulation of airlines. No one can say that travelling on an American airline these days is a comfortable experience. As more and more companies get into the airline business the service gets less and less. It becomes more of a no-frills service. Inside the passenger cabin that is not such a problem. But when economies are made on safety one has to be very worried.
The figures in the United States give cause for concern. For instance, in 1979 the Federal Aviation Administration had 2,000 inspectors monitoring 237 air carriers. In 1984 it had 1,300 inspectors for 407 air carriers. In Canada, the Auditor General reported in 1985 that Transport Canada was unable to inspect all air carriers in its jurisdiction once a year.
If the Government encourages small aircraft companies to come into existence, not necessarily well-capitalized ones with new equipment, and not necessarily well-staffed, what guarantees of safety will we have? The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has been telling Canadians that airfares on Canadian airlines will drop as a result of deregulation. How will airline fares drop? Clearly, only if staff are laid off and if services are reduced. There is nothing in the Bill to guarantee that there will be the same concentration on air safety as we have had in the past.
For all those reasons I regret that the Government has chosen to introduce closure on this Bill. I hope that even at this stage it might reconsider and be prepared to examine some of the very thoughtful and careful amendments that have been laid before the House.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate. I want to start out by indicating that I think the questions that need to be put to the House are these. Why is the Government moving to cut off debate? Why is the Government using the heavy hand of closure in order to rush this Bill through the House? Why is it limiting debate? Why does it no longer want to hear from Members of Parliament with regard to transportation and deregulation? Why does it not want to hear from Canadians? Why has it closed its ears instead of giving this legislation the type of thorough and full debate that it needs? Is it simply trying to sweep the potential consequences from this deregulation package under the rug? Does it not want to look at possible implications of what it is doing before it gives it the full force of law?
This leaves one with the impression that what it has tried to do is force-feed Canadians with its particular brand of free enterprise deregulation ideology instead of encouraging a full and comprehensive debate on the legislation that is before the House, instead of allowing for public input and instead of allowing for this legislation to be examined in a full and complete way.
Just what is the approach that the Government is taking to deregulation? I think there are a number of options that the Government could look at. One of the ways it might approach the question of regulation of transportation, whether it is in the air, by way of trucking or other means, is to simply maintain the status quo.
Not being an expert in the transportation field, I am unaware of the number of years that the present legislation has been in place. Certainly after legislation has been in place for a number of years there is probably a need for review. Circumstances change. The economy changes. The needs of people change to some degree.
The Government could have taken the approach of freezing things as they now stand and simply continuing the status quo. Another approach would be to eliminate any effective regulation. It is this latter approach that the Government has adopted. In doing so, it has dressed it up with the fine-sounding slogan, "freedom to move."
Obviously, every Canadian is a lover of freedom. Rather than being frank with the Canadian public and coming straight out and telling the public that it is eliminating any effective regulation in the transportation sector in order to meet the concerns of the industry itself and the consumers of transportation, it attaches a nice public relations-type slogan to the Bill, calling it Freedom to Move.
So, we have those two approaches, continuing the status quo, or eliminating any effective regulation in transportation. But, were those the only choices available to the Government? Are those the only routes available?
When listening to the government Members one gets the impression that it was a choice only between the status quo, no change at all, and radical change, a radical cutting away of the regulatory environment relating to safety and service, consumer needs, and the needs of the industry itself.
I suggest that the Government had another option. It could continue the debate on this measure in the House; it could continue the examination of the regulatory environment that exists in this country.
The whole subject could be approached from the point of view of re-regulation. In other words, we could examine the present regime in the light of present-day requirements. Such a course would result in a rational and reasonable approach to the regulation of the transportation sector. Instead of Bill C-18, we could have had a participatory approach. The Government could have said to Canadians, "We have confidence in your opinions, and in the opinions of your representatives. We want to ensure that all Canadians have an opportunity for input into the whole question of regulation of the transportation sector. To that end, it is our intention to canvass the opinion of Canadians, regardless of where they live."
That is an alternate approach to the one taken by the
Government. Instead of looking for the alternative, the
June 15, 1987

Government has decided to close down debate. It has chosen to try to force-feed Canadians a particularly ideological point of view on regulation.
Ordinary Canadians do have some legitimate concerns when it comes to the transportation industry in this country. There are good and valid reasons why the present regulatory regime has been built up. There are good reasons why we seek to regulate transportation in this country. One reason, of course, is the whole question of safety.
As a consumer, one cannot check out every carrier that one may want to use for vacation or business travel. One simply cannot investigate each carrier in order to assure oneself of one's safety in transit. One of the legitimate purposes of regulation is to ensure the safety of the traveller.
When regulation is virtually eliminated and there is put in its stead an Adam Smith survival-of-the-fittest approach to competition, an environment of cutthroat competition, there is a great deal of temptation on the part of those seeking to survive to cut corners. Someone has to be looking over the shoulders of the industry to ensure that, in cutting corners, the safety of the traveller is not jeopardized. We need to have someone who will ensure that safety standards are of the highest possible.
These are the kinds of concerns that must be dealt with in the debate on the regulation of the transportation sector. The cutting off of debate can only result in there being an inadequate response to these concerns.
Canadians are concerned about the whole question of price. The Government indicates that we are going to have a honeymoon with regard to price; that we are going to get very low air fares. The impression is that one is going to be able to travel almost free. Well, while there may be a honeymoon with regard to air fares between such centres as Toronto and Montreal, the high density areas of the country, I doubt very much that there will be any such honeymoon in respect of regional centres such as Winnipeg. As well, a honeymoon is a short-term proposition. We all know that. What about the long term? What are the long-term consequences for price in a deregulated environment?
In that regard, let me quote from an article which deals with some of the research on deregulation in the United States. I quote from an article in Traffic World of April 20, 1987:
Deregulation has spurred rail, motor and airline carriers toward an "oligopoly in each of the modes," said L. Leslie Waters, Indiana University professor emeritus of transportation and business history-
Up to now, there has been "an enormous volume of rate cutting and many have been pleased; we as shippers have been enjoying a lengthy period of reasonably good service at moderate rates in relation to the economy," -But he warned, "shippers had better enjoy it, because the forces of oligopoly will prevail, and even without overt collusion, rates will increase and shippers will be lobbying for reimposition of regulations-just as some are now in the case of railroads."
What Professor Waters is saying is that while we may get lower prices at the beginning of deregulation, given that the ownership of the industry will fall into fewer and fewer hands,
National Transportation Act, 1986
which is what I understand the term "oligopoly" to mean, prices will eventually increase.
These are the kinds of questions that have to be answered before this Bill passes into law. In terms of the situation south of the border, we hear that the Americans are getting a good deal on price. Well, the U.S. presents a much different circumstance from that which exists in Canada. We are walking blind if we think that deregulation will have a similar impact in Canada to that in the U.S., with its much larger population and much different geography.
In summary, what I am saying is that the Government, rather than closing off debate on this measure, cutting off the input of Canadians, should be opening up this legislation to further examination. Canadians have real concerns in the area of safety, in the area of price. The Government should permit the continuation of the discussion until those concerns are met in an adequate way, rather than pushing this legislation through.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to relate the importance of the economic benefits which will follow the passage of the transportation Bills, but after listening to Hon. Members opposite, I am mindful of the ancient quote, "Nero fiddles while Rome burns".
I do not have to say anything to Hon. Members of the House about the great economic benefits and importance of freer trade to Canada as an exporting nation, nor do I have to point out that our higher standard of living is primarily based upon our export trade. We in this country are, perhaps more than any other country, concerned about the cost of transporting our goods to market, be they manufactured goods or raw products. Goodness knows, many of us are still hewers of wood and drawers of water, vendors of raw resources. The problem is that the world around us is becoming much more competitive. As each country becomes more competitive minded, it looks at ways and means of reducing its costs. Canada cannot do otherwise. Canada must do likewise, because the cost of getting goods to market is of extreme importance.
These reforms are needed because the existing economic regulatory scheme for transportation, introduced over 20 years ago, now impedes rather than helps our competitive growth. Competition has been stifled while the regulatory process has become cumbersome, time consuming, and costly. Put simply, the market-place demands that economic regulation catch up to this reality.
If we did not manufacture and produce or sell what we manufacture and produce, perhaps we would not have to be concerned about the carrier. However, the shippers are saying, "Get on with the job that you started over two years ago". The Coalition of Concerned Shippers and shippers generally, particularly rail captive shippers, cry out, "How long will we continue to be so captive?" In their great numbers they are saying, "We support the Government in its desire to introduce

June 15, 1987
regulatory reform so that transportation will carry our goods to market at a cheaper, more economic cost".
Undoubtedly shippers whole-heartedly support the early passage of Bill C-18. Shippers, industrial associations, and exporters urge early passage of the Bill. Every day that the Bill is not the law of the land means additional cost to them.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext: Baloney.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-18
speechtext:
I have heard that comment before.
I am somewhat nonplused by the air deregulation comments of the Official Opposition in particular. We are already embarked upon a smooth, final approach to the deregulation process. No new drastic change is anticipated in the way that Canadian carriers will do business safely and efficiently.
While on the other side of the river in the United States the consolidation or rationalization process may have caused some concern, it should not do so here. Canadian Airlines International Limited has simply replaced Canadian Pacific Airlines. Along with Air Canada it is assembling rival networks and is acquiring feeder lines to establish two main national carriers. This consolidation started to take place prior to the introduction of Bill C-18 with the implementation of regulation and the encouragement and otherwise of a former Minister of Transport who is now in the Official Opposition. The process was initiated and ongoing, and now it is being openly proposed by the Government in this Bill. It seems somewhat inconsistent to hear the former Minister of Transport urge Members of Parliament to delay the process which he started.
Deregulation has taken place in all modes of transportation in the United States. Each day the Americans draw business away from our carriers. The provisions contained in the Bill will make our railways more competitive with one another. Indeed, we hope that with the passage of the Bill they will be more competitive with that major U.S. carrier, Burlington Northern, which is competitive when it comes to carrying our resources.
As the Bill will show, shippers will have more competitive access to our railways. There will be a continuance of the economic viability of Canadian railways. The Bill strikes at the right, fair, and just balance.
Turning to truckers, that segment of the transportation industry will be dealt with more fully in Bill C-19. However, let me say that in Alberta they have played successfully with the deregulation process and Canadian truckers have not done badly in trans-border markets. One southern Ontario carrier, an established truck carrier, put it the following way: "Deregulation as proposed would eliminate much of the unnecessary red tape and the delays in getting licences and will create a more efficient transportation system".
I should like to conclude by referring to a factor of national concern-safety. It has been raised time and time again by members of the Opposition. There is no doubt that those persons who operate in any segment of the transportation
industry will put safety first. As the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and the earlier Minister of Transport both said, safety will be a priority concern of the Government. No step in the reregulatory process will endanger any safety factor in any segment of transportation. We have acted and will continue to act in the interests of improving air safety. There is no question; safety will not be impaired by reason of the passage of these transportation Bills.
I urge, along with other members of the Government, the early passage of Bill C-18 so that our carriers can have an equal opportunity to be competitive with national carriers of the United States and our shippers, whoever they are, will be able to get their products to market at a competitive price.
